provenance.other: “with one voice” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 24:3 and Acts 19:34. Acts 19:34 is the Ephesian mob shouting for Diana; Exodus 24:3 is the people of Israel ratifying the covenant at Sinai.
provenance.significance: Benjamin's assembly is a covenant-ratification scene, and it borrows the sentence that ratifies the Sinai covenant. The metalepsis is exact: at Exodus 24:3 the one voice says 'All the words which the LORD hath said will we do', and two chapters later, at Mosiah 5:2, the one voice will say 'we believe all the words which thou hast spoken unto us'. The KJV's only covenantal use of the phrase is the one the Book of Mormon has taken, and it has taken it twice, at the two ends of the same assembly.

4:2.note: 'And they all cried aloud with one voice, saying, O have mercy…'. The phrase is a KJV rarity with two homes, and only one of them is a covenant scene. Everything around it presses the same way: a people gathered before their leader, prostrate, answering as one, and about to bind themselves by oath — which is Exodus 24. The 1830 wording adds 'aloud', which is in neither KJV verse and is the Book of Mormon's own.
4:2.text: And Moses came and told the people all the words of the LORD, and all the judgments: and all the people answered with one voice, and said, All the words which the LORD hath said will we do.

provenance.other: “purifying their hearts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 15:9, where the purifying agent is faith.
provenance.significance: Acts 15:9 is Peter's argument at the Jerusalem council that God made no difference between Jew and Gentile because he purified Gentile hearts by faith. Benjamin's multitude is a single covenant people, not a disputed one — but the sentence they use to ask for a clean heart is the sentence the New Testament uses to abolish the distinction between insiders and outsiders, and Mosiah 3:20 has just promised that the knowledge of the Saviour will 'spread throughout every nation, kindred, tongue and people'.

4:2.note: 'That we may receive forgiveness of our sins, and our hearts may be purified: for we believe in Jesus Christ.' Two clauses, and each is a New Testament rarity. The purification of the heart by belief is Acts 15:9's exact formula — purified hearts, and faith as the instrument — and the KJV has no other verse that puts those two together in those words. The Old Testament asks for a clean heart (Psalm 51:10) but never purifies one by faith.
4:2.text: And put no difference between us and them, purifying their hearts by faith.

provenance.other: “receive forgiveness of sins” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 26:18. The KJV's usual idiom is 'remission of sins' (Matthew 26:28, Acts 2:38, Acts 10:43), which Mosiah 4:3 uses in the very next verse.
provenance.significance: The pairing matters more than either half. Mosiah 4 reaches Acts 26 twice: 'receive forgiveness of … sins' here, and 'truth and soberness' — also a KJV singleton — at 4:15, seven verses further on in Paul's defence before Agrippa. A chapter that touches one page of the New Testament twice is using that page, not remembering a phrase.

4:2.note: 'That we may receive forgiveness of our sins.' The KJV normally says 'remission', and Mosiah 4:3 duly says 'remission' one sentence later; the switch to 'forgiveness' here lands on the one verse where the KJV says it that way. Acts 26:18 is Paul reciting his commission — eyes opened, darkness to light, the power of Satan — which is the movement Benjamin's multitude has just undergone in 4:1-2.
4:2.text: To open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins, and inheritance among them which are sanctified by faith that is in me.

provenance.other: “the goodness of God” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 52:1 and Romans 2:4. Only Romans 2:4 attaches it to longsuffering and to repentance; “goodness and forbearance and longsuffering” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 2:4.
provenance.significance: Paul's sentence is a reproach — 'despisest thou the riches of his goodness … not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?' — put to people who presume on mercy. Benjamin turns the reproach into a diagnosis of what has just happened in front of him: the knowledge of the goodness of God has led these people to repentance, on the ground, in one verse. Recover Romans 2 and the passage reads as Paul's rhetorical question answered in the affirmative by a whole city.

4:5.note: 'If the knowledge of the goodness of God at this time, hath awakened you to a sense of your nothingness.' The phrase recurs at 4:6 and 4:11 and each time it drags Romans 2:4's other terms with it: 4:6 lists 'his patience, and his long suffering', which is Paul's 'forbearance and longsuffering', and the whole sequence is the goodness of God producing repentance. Two KJV verses have the phrase and only one has the argument.
4:5.text: Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?

provenance.other: “prepared for you from the foundation of the world” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 25:34. The KJV never writes 'prepared from the foundation of the world' without the intervening 'for you'; the nearest other verse to join preparation to that phrase is Revelation 13:8's 'the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world'.
provenance.significance: This is the first of three visits Benjamin's sermon pays to Matthew 25:31-46. Here the atonement is what was prepared from the foundation of the world; at 4:26 the works of mercy are Matthew's own list, hungry, naked, sick; at 5:9-10 the saved are found at the right hand of God and the rest on the left. Matthew 25 supplies this discourse with its eschatology, its ethics and its stage directions, and the borrowing at 4:6 is the one that sets the frame — Benjamin has substituted 'the atonement' for Matthew's 'kingdom' in the King's own sentence.

4:6.note: 'The atonement which hath been prepared from the foundation of the world, that thereby salvation might come.' Six of the seven words are Matthew 25:34's and in Matthew's order; what changes is the thing prepared. The KJV has 'foundation of the world' in six verses but only one where something is prepared from it, and that one is the judgment scene this chapter goes on to quote twice more. Revelation 13:8 stands behind the substitution — it is where the KJV puts an atoning act at the foundation of the world.
4:6.text: Then shall the King say unto them on his right hand, Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world:

provenance.other: “believe that he is” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 11:6. The construction is peculiar English — an absolute 'is' with no predicate — and it exists in the KJV only here.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 11:6 is the hinge of the chapter on faith: it defines the minimum content of belief and then says God rewards those who seek him. Benjamin takes the minimum and expands it into a creed — he is, he created all things, he has all wisdom and all power — and then, at 4:10, adds the thing Hebrews leaves implicit: 'if you believe all these things, see that ye do them.' The suppressed half of Hebrews 11:6, that God 'is a rewarder', is what Benjamin's next twenty verses argue about beggars and substance.

4:9.note: 'Believe in God; believe that he is, and that he created all things.' Four words, but they are the four rarest possible: the KJV's only bare predicative 'believe that he is', taken with its following 'and that he', which the dossier's n-gram stream caught as a seven-word run. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold, and not one of his quotations; the case rests on absolute rarity, not on length. Note that the 1830 'hath all wisdom' was smoothed to 'has' in 1920, moving the sentence away from the KJV's register.
4:9.text: But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him.

provenance.other: “calling on the name of the Lord” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 22:16. The KJV's other forms are all finite — 'call on the name of the LORD' (Genesis 4:26, Psalm 116:17, Joel 2:32, Acts 2:21) — and the participial phrase is Ananias's alone.
provenance.significance: Ananias's words are spoken to a man who has just been struck down, blinded, and told to arise; Benjamin's are spoken to a multitude that has just fallen to the earth and been raised by a remission of sins. The suppressed half of Acts 22:16 is 'arise, and be baptized, and wash away thy sins' — which is the sequence Mosiah 6:1-2 will complete when Benjamin takes the names of everyone who has entered the covenant.

4:11.note: 'Calling on the name of the Lord daily, and standing steadfastly in the faith of that which is to come.' The participle is the tell. Every other KJV occurrence conjugates the verb; only Acts 22:16 leaves it hanging as a description of a posture, which is exactly how Benjamin uses it — not an act to perform once but a daily condition. 'Standing steadfastly in the faith' anticipates 5:15's 'steadfast and immovable', where the source is 1 Corinthians 15:58.
4:11.text: And now why tarriest thou? arise, and be baptized, and wash away thy sins, calling on the name of the Lord.

provenance.other: “grow in the knowledge” occurs in no KJV verse; 2 Peter 3:18 reads 'grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour'. “the knowledge of the glory” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Habakkuk 2:14 and 2 Corinthians 4:6.
provenance.significance: The verse fuses the only two KJV idioms available to it — Peter's imperative to grow in knowledge and Paul's 'light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ' — and the fusion is what makes it a Book of Mormon sentence rather than a quotation. Where Paul locates the glory in Christ's face, Benjamin locates it in creation: 'the knowledge of the glory of Him that created you'.

4:12.note: 'Ye shall grow in the knowledge of the glory of Him that created you.' Neither source supplies the whole clause and neither is deniable in it: the verb and its object are 2 Peter 3:18's, the genitive chain is 2 Corinthians 4:6's. Recorded at moderate because a composite of two common idioms is a weaker thing than a singleton, and because 'grow in the knowledge' as such is in no KJV verse.
4:12.text: But grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. To him be glory both now and for ever. Amen.

provenance.other: “live peaceably” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 12:18. “dues” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 13:7. “render to every man according to” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Proverbs 24:12 and Romans 2:6.
provenance.significance: The verse is built out of a continuous stretch of Romans, in Paul's own order: recompense no man evil for evil (12:17), live peaceably with all men (12:18), render to all their dues (13:7). The Book of Mormon has not taken a phrase from Romans; it has taken a paragraph's argument and compressed it into one sentence, and the compression preserves the sequence. That is the strongest kind of evidence the sequence subscore can carry.

4:13.note: 'Ye will not have a mind to injure one another, but to live peaceably, and to render to every man according to that which is his due.' Three clauses and each is Paul's. The mediation test is decisive and it is decisive twice over: 'render to every man according to' is shared by Proverbs 24:12 and Romans 2:6, so on its own the verse cannot choose between Testaments — but Mosiah's object is neither Proverbs' 'works' nor Romans 2:6's 'deeds'. It is 'his due', which is Romans 13:7's word and appears nowhere else in the KJV. The Book of Mormon has read Romans 2:6 with Romans 13:7 and taken the noun from the second.
4:13.text: Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour.

provenance.other: “enemy of all righteousness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 13:10. The Book of Mormon has 'enemy to all righteousness', which occurs in no KJV verse — the preposition is its only departure.
provenance.significance: Acts 13:10 is Paul blinding Elymas the sorcerer, and the epithet comes in a series: 'O full of all subtilty and all mischief, thou child of the devil, thou enemy of all righteousness.' Benjamin has taken the second and third members of that series and kept them together — his warning is about children who 'serve the Devil' and about the devil as 'an enemy to all righteousness'. The 'child of the devil' that Paul spat at a magician has become, in Benjamin's mouth, a thing parents can let their own children become by neglect.

4:14.note: 'He being an enemy to all righteousness.' A KJV singleton with one preposition changed, and the change is the kind that a memory makes and a transcription does not. What secures the link is not the phrase alone but its company: Acts 13:10's 'child of the devil' sits four words away from it, and Mosiah 4:14's clause about children who 'serve the Devil' sits eleven words away from the borrowing. Two halves of one verse, in one sentence, with the same subject.
4:14.text: And said, O full of all subtilty and all mischief, thou child of the devil, thou enemy of all righteousness, wilt thou not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord?

provenance.other: “truth and soberness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 26:25. 'Soberness' itself occurs only there; the KJV's usual noun is 'sobriety' (1 Timothy 2:9, 2:15).
provenance.significance: Paul says it to Festus, who has just shouted that he is mad: 'I am not mad, most noble Festus; but speak forth the words of truth and soberness.' The words are a defence of a man accused of raving in front of a king. Benjamin, speaking in front of his own people from a tower, tells them to teach their children to walk in that same speech. Read with 4:2's borrowing from Acts 26:18, the chapter has been in Paul's Agrippa speech twice, and it takes both times from Paul's own words rather than from the narrative around them.

4:15.note: 'Ye will teach them to walk in the ways of truth and soberness.' The pairing is a KJV singleton and the second noun is a KJV hapax, which is as much rarity evidence as a four-word phrase can carry. The n-gram stream found this one and ranked it low; it is one of the chapter's cleaner borrowings.
4:15.text: But he said, I am not mad, most noble Festus; but speak forth the words of truth and soberness.

provenance.other: “lifteth up the beggar” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 2:8. 'Beggar' is a rare KJV word — 1 Samuel 2:8 and Luke 16:20, 16:22 — and Mosiah 4 uses it five times in eight verses.
provenance.significance: Hannah's song is the KJV's one place where a beggar is raised from the dunghill and set among princes, and it is sung at the founding of Israel's monarchy by the mother of the prophet who will anoint its kings. Benjamin is a king, on a tower, at the moment of handing the kingdom to his son, telling the assembled kingdom that they are all beggars. The reversal Hannah sings about — princes and beggars changing places — is what Benjamin performs on himself in 2:14 and asserts of everyone here.

4:19.note: 'For behold, are we not all beggars?' The word is the evidence. The KJV has three verses with a beggar in them and only one where the beggar is the subject of a theology rather than a parable, and it is the song Benjamin's whole sermon on kingship and dependence is shaped like. Volume is thin — no clause is reproduced — but the vocabulary is rare and the thematic coherence is total, which is the shape Hays's criteria give a genuine echo as against a quotation.
4:19.text: He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth up the beggar from the dunghill, to set them among princes, and to make them inherit the throne of glory: for the pillars of the earth are the LORD’s, and he hath set the world upon them.

4:20.text: And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance.

provenance.other: 'Utterance' occurs in five KJV verses, and Acts 2:4 is the only one where the Spirit is its giver. “poured out my spirit” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 39:29; Acts 2:17-18, quoting Joel, has 'I will pour out of my Spirit'.
provenance.significance: The scene is Pentecost run backwards. In Acts 2 the Spirit is poured out, the mouths are opened, and utterance is given; in Mosiah 4:20 the Spirit is poured out, the mouths are stopped, and utterance cannot be found. Both crowds are prostrate and both are overwhelmed, and the Book of Mormon has kept every element of the Pentecost sequence while inverting its one distinctive effect. A speechless Pentecost is a considered thing to write, not an accident of vocabulary.

4:20.note: 'He hath poured out his spirit upon you … and hath caused that your mouths should be stopped, that ye could not find utterance.' The two rare terms of Acts 2 are both here, in Acts's order, and the second is negated. 'Utterance' is not common KJV English — five verses in the whole Bible — and only Acts 2:4 makes the Spirit its source, which is the connection the negation depends on. Filed at moderate because the shared wording is two words and the argument rests on the inversion.

provenance.other: “believing ye shall receive” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 21:22 (the KJV punctuates 'believing, ye shall receive'). “ask in faith” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, James 1:6. Mark 11:24's parallel reads differently — 'believe that ye receive them, and ye shall have them'.
provenance.significance: The mediation is decidable inside the New Testament. Matthew and Mark carry the same saying and word it differently, and Mosiah 4:21 has Matthew's participle and Matthew's future — not Mark's 'believe that ye receive'. Then James 1:6 supplies the qualifier Matthew lacks, 'ask in faith', which is what lets Benjamin add his own 'whatsoever ye ask that is right'. A promise given without limit in Matthew is being fenced by James before it is used.

4:21.note: 'Doth grant unto you whatsoever ye ask that is right, in faith, believing that ye shall receive.' Matthew's clause arrives whole, with 'that' inserted; the surrounding conditions are James's and Benjamin's own. The argument the borrowing serves is not about prayer at all — it is the premise of an a fortiori about almsgiving: if God gives you whatever you ask, how ought you to give to one another. The New Testament's most unqualified promise has been made into an obligation to the poor.
4:21.text: And all things, whatsoever ye shall ask in prayer, believing, ye shall receive.

4:23.text: But Peter said unto him, Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money.

provenance.other: “perish with thee” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 8:20. The KJV has no other sentence in which a man's money or goods are consigned to perish along with the man.
provenance.significance: Peter says it to Simon the sorcerer, who offered money for the gift of God. Benjamin says it of a rich man who refused money to a beggar. The two errors are opposite — one buys what cannot be bought, the other withholds what was never his — and the Book of Mormon has answered both with the same sentence, which is exactly the kind of unstated correspondence Hays calls metalepsis. The verse just before Benjamin's, 4:22, has already said that the substance 'doth not belong to you, but to God': Simon's mistake was to think the things of God purchasable, and Benjamin's rich man's is to think the things of God his own.

4:23.note: 'Wo be unto that man, for his substance shall perish with him.' Not a verbatim run — 'substance' for 'money', 'him' for 'thee' — but the construction is a KJV singleton and there is nothing else in the Bible it could be. Acts 13:10's 'enemy to all righteousness' at 4:14 and Acts 8:20 here put the chapter in Acts's apostolic-rebuke scenes twice; the register of Benjamin's denunciations is Lukan.

provenance.other: “I was sick and ye visited me” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 25:36. Isaiah 58:7 is the standing Old Testament candidate for a list of this kind and it will not do the work: it has bread for the hungry and a covering for the naked, but no sick and no visiting, and its verb for the naked is 'cover', not 'clothe'.
provenance.significance: Benjamin's list is Matthew's list, minus the stranger and the prisoner and plus 'administering to their relief, both spiritually and temporally' — an addition that turns a judgment scene into a welfare instruction. Recover the context and the borrowing is doing what Matthew 25 does: the works are the criterion of the judgment, which is why the chapter has already taken 'prepared from the foundation of the world' from Matthew 25:34 at 4:6 and will take the right hand and the left from Matthew 25:33 at 5:9-10. Three separate borrowings from one pericope, spread across two chapters of one sermon.

4:26.note: 'Such as feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, visiting the sick.' The mediation test decides it: run Mosiah 4:26 against Isaiah 58:7 and Matthew 25:35-36 and the Old Testament candidate fails on two words the Book of Mormon has and Isaiah does not — 'sick' and 'visiting' — while the verb applied to the naked is Matthew's 'clothe' and not Isaiah's 'cover'. Nominalizing Matthew's first-person narrative into a list of gerunds is the reason this is catalogued as a paraphrastic quotation rather than a verbatim one; below Skousen's threshold, and none of his thirty-six.
4:26.text: Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me.

provenance.other: “receiveth the prize” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 9:24. “the prize” occurs in exactly two, 1 Corinthians 9:24 and Philippians 3:14. The KJV never uses 'win' of the prize; that verb is the Book of Mormon's.
provenance.significance: Paul's footrace is a warning that only one runner receives the prize, so run to obtain. Benjamin inverts the pace and keeps the image: 'it is not requisite that a man should run faster than what he hath strength', and then, in the same breath, 'that thereby he might win the prize'. The suppressed context is 1 Corinthians 9:27, where Paul keeps his body under lest he himself be a castaway — the same anxiety about running past one's own strength, reached by the opposite counsel.

4:27.note: 'It is not requisite that a man should run faster than what he hath strength … that thereby he might win the prize.' Running and the prize in one sentence is Pauline and, in the KJV, nearly unique to this verse. The 1830 reading 'faster than what he hath strength' was tidied in 1920 by deleting 'what', which removes the awkward relative that makes the sentence sound like the KJV in the first place.
4:27.text: Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain.

provenance.other: “decently and in order” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 14:40, which is the KJV's only instruction that things be 'done in order' at all.
provenance.significance: Both of this verse's borrowings come from one letter, and the chapter's argument is the same as Paul's in 1 Corinthians 12-14: gifts and works are to be distributed and exercised in proportion and in order, not in excess. Benjamin's 'all things must be done in order' closes a paragraph about giving in the way Paul's closes a chapter about speaking.

4:27.note: 'See that all these things are done in wisdom and order … therefore, all things must be done in order.' The formula is stated twice in one verse, and the KJV states it once in the whole Bible. The n-gram stream proposed Mark 4:11 for the same run ('all these things are done in'), which is the trap the pilot named: the longest match is not the source. Mark's next word is 'parables'.
4:27.text: Let all things be done decently and in order.

provenance.other: “borrow ought of his neighbour” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 22:14 — the Covenant Code's law of bailment.
provenance.significance: Benjamin has been legislating like Moses for twenty verses, and here he legislates in Moses' own words, from the code that immediately precedes the covenant-ratification scene his people re-enacted at 4:2. Exodus 22 is the law; Exodus 24 is the assembly that swears to keep it. Mosiah 4 has now used both, in that order. But the sanction has changed: Exodus 22:14 says the borrower 'shall surely make it good', a restitution; Benjamin says 'thou shalt commit sin', and adds that the defaulter may make his neighbour sin too. A civil liability has become a spiritual one.

4:28.note: 'Whosoever among you that borroweth of his neighbor, should return the thing that he borroweth.' The subject, verb and indirect object are Exodus 22:14's, which is the KJV's only sentence about borrowing from a neighbour. The transformation is the finding: the Covenant Code assesses damages, Benjamin assesses guilt, and he extends the guilt to the lender's own sin — which is not in Exodus at all.
4:28.text: And if a man borrow ought of his neighbour, and it be hurt, or die, the owner thereof being not with it, he shall surely make it good.

provenance.other: “continue in the faith” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 14:22 and Colossians 1:23. Only Colossians 1:23 goes on to 'which ye have heard', which occurs in exactly three KJV verses (Colossians 1:23, 1 John 2:7, 1 John 2:24).
provenance.significance: Colossians 1:23 makes continuance conditional — 'if ye continue in the faith grounded and settled, and be not moved away' — and it is that conditional, not the exhortation, that Benjamin ends his sermon on: continue, or 'ye must perish'. The suppressed half of Paul's verse, 'grounded and settled … be not moved away', surfaces one chapter later as 'steadfast and immovable' at 5:15, where the wording is 1 Corinthians 15:58's. Benjamin's peroration and his benediction are built from the same Pauline idea reached through two different verses.

4:30.note: 'Continue in the faith of what ye have heard concerning the coming of our Lord, even unto the end of your lives, ye must perish.' Two of Colossians 1:23's clauses stand in one Book of Mormon clause, in Paul's order, and Acts 14:22 — the other verse with 'continue in the faith' — has neither the hearing nor the condition. The phrase has already been used once in the chapter, at 4:6; this is the occurrence that carries the source, because it is the one that brings 'which ye have heard' with it.
4:30.text: If ye continue in the faith grounded and settled, and be not moved away from the hope of the gospel, which ye have heard, and which was preached to every creature which is under heaven; whereof I Paul am made a minister;
